REP: Emily, thanks for the time. I'd love to hear how the start of the season is going before I talk about anything we sell. How's it looking so far?
CUSTOMER: Busy. We're already seeing a lot of coughs and sore throats, and it's only September. The schools went back three weeks ago, and it's like clockwork.
REP: What are those customers asking you for?
CUSTOMER: Mostly what to take. Some of them want antibiotics without seeing anyone, and I have to explain that's not how it works. They've usually tried everything on the cold aisle by the time they get to me.
REP: How do those conversations usually end?
CUSTOMER: Not great. I tell them to see a doctor, they tell me they can't get an appointment until next week, and they leave frustrated. Sometimes they buy something, sometimes they don't. The worst is the parents. They just want to know if their kid can go to school tomorrow, and I can't tell them.
REP: If you could give them a definite answer right here, what would that be worth to you?
CUSTOMER: A lot, in goodwill. But I'm not sure people around here would come to a pharmacy for a test. This is a small town. People are used to going to Dr. Hale for everything.
REP: That's a reasonable doubt, and small towns are different. When Dr. Hale's office is full, where do people go?
CUSTOMER: They wait, mostly. Or they drive forty minutes to the urgent care in Millerton. In the winter, with the roads, a lot of them just don't go at all.
REP: So the people who can't get in with Dr. Hale either wait or drive forty minutes. That's exactly the group pharmacy testing serves. In towns your size, our stores average six to eight tests a week in flu season, mostly from people who would otherwise have driven or waited. And some of our pharmacists set up a referral arrangement with the local practice, so a positive strep result goes straight to the doctor's office for a prescription. Do you think Dr. Hale's office might welcome that?
CUSTOMER: Actually, they might. They're drowning. His nurse told me last week they're turning people away. Dr. Hale is close to retirement, and they haven't been able to hire another doctor.
REP: That's a great opening. What would concern you about running the tests yourself?
CUSTOMER: I'm the only pharmacist most days. If I'm in the consultation room swabbing someone, who's checking prescriptions? I can't leave the counter for fifteen minutes at a time. The line would be out the door.
REP: That's the right question to ask. Who's working with you on a typical weekday?
CUSTOMER: Two techs. One of them, Jordan, is certified and very sharp. She's been with me five years and she already handles most of the inventory.
REP: Then Jordan would do the swabs. In most states a trained technician can collect the sample, and the reader runs by itself for about ten minutes. You'd spend about a minute reviewing the result and talking to the patient, so you'd only leave the counter for that one minute. Does that work with how your counter runs?
CUSTOMER: A minute I can do. Jordan would be thrilled, honestly. She's been asking for more responsibility, and I've been worried about losing her to the hospital, so this might actually help me keep her.
REP: Then let's set it up. I'll call Dr. Hale's office manager this week to introduce the referral idea, if that's okay with you, and I'll come back Tuesday the 29th at eleven to sign the CLIA packet with you and schedule Jordan's training. Does that work?
CUSTOMER: Yes. Tuesday the 29th at eleven. And please do call the office. Tell them I sent you.
REP: I will. I'll send you a recap this afternoon with everything we agreed.
CUSTOMER: Thanks, Daniel.
